title: Adaptive tiling and clock profiles for mixed GPU fleets (A100/H100/L4/MI300)
content:
Summary:
This draft outlines an operational guidance and runtime-level design for adaptive model tiling (quant/block tiling), kernel-selection preemption windows, and per-GPU clock/power profiles across our mixed fleet (NVIDIA A100, H100, L4 and AMD MI300). The goal is to reduce p99 and mean latency variance for mixed real-time workloads while optimizing cost (watts/token) and preserving KV cache hit behavior. This doc focuses on tuning knobs and an automated calibration flow rather than re-architecting the runtime.

Context & motivation:
- We run mixed latency-sensitive and throughput-batched inference on heterogeneous fleets. Static clock/power settings tuned for throughput (high P-state) are suboptimal for latency spikes and small-batch interactive requests.
- Kernel selection and tiling (how we quantize / tile matrix multiplies and how we choose kernels for different sequence lengths) interact with clocking: a kernel that is compute-bound on high clocks may become memory-bound under power caps and vice versa.
- KV cache locality is sensitive to how we partition GPU memory (tiling) and how many concurrent kernels are scheduled; poor tiling can cause eviction storms that invalidate cache benefits for chat sessions.

Goals (measurable):
1) Reduce p99 latency tail for <32-token interactive requests by >= 15% on average under mixed load.
2) Reduce average power draw per token by >= 8% for steady-state mixed workloads.
3) Avoid KV cache eviction rate increase > 2% compared to baseline.
4) Provide a reproducible calibration flow to produce per-instance clock+tiling profiles for deployed hosts.

Design principles:
- Conservative default: runtime ships with a safe default per-GPU profile (see table) that prioritizes latency stability for interactive classes.
- Workload-aware adaptation: profiles adjust based on observed qps/sequence-length distribution and KV-hotset pressure.
- Non-invasive rollout: per-host calibration jobs run offline and produce named profiles; runtime can shift profiles via rollout policies (canary, gradual).
- Observable and reversible: expose telemetry (kernel choices, GPU clocks, TDP, memory pressure, kv-eviction counters) and automatic rollback triggers.

High-level approach:
1) Profile: microbench exact matrix sizes and quant modes on each GPU type using representative sequence lengths and batch sizes. Capture FLOP/s, bandwidth utilisation, kernel latency distributions, and memory working set per request type.
2) Calibrate: run an automated sweep over clock ranges and power caps to find knee points where latency or watts/token materially change.
3) Synthesize profiles: select a small set of profiles (low-latency, balanced, low-power) per host type and name them (e.g., a100-latency-v1).
4) Runtime policy: choose profile by request class (interactive vs batch), and dynamically flip profile at host-level using gradual rollouts.

Microbench methodology (recommended):
- Inputs: model, tokenizer, seq-lengths {8, 32, 128, 512}, batch sizes {1,4,8,16}, quant modes (fp16, int8/llm.int8 when available).
- Metrics: median latency, p90, p99, throughput, measured GPU power (nvidia-smi/rocm tools), sustained SM utilization, measured DRAM bandwidth, KV cache working set estimate, memory alloc failure/eviction events.
- Sweep variables: application clocks (sm/mem or analogous), power cap (TDP cap where available), CUDA MPS vs individualized scheduling, kernel selection flags e.g., fused attention vs fallback.

Per-GPU guidance (summary table):
- NVIDIA A100 (40/80GB):
  * Baseline profile: a100-balanced-v1 -> stable clocks: SM 1375 MHz / Mem 877 MHz, no hard power cap (allow system governor). This balances throughput and avoids thermal throttling under sustained batches.
  * Latency profile: a100-latency-v1 -> set SM lock to 1650 MHz (if supported) and a conservative power cap of -10% off nameplate TDP; this reduces time-to-first-token for short sequences because increased single-kernel throughput reduces kernel scheduling contention.
  * Power-saver profile: a100-saver-v1 -> SM 1150 MHz / Mem 877 MHz + lower power cap (-20%). Use for background batch only.
  * Notes: A100 shows a strong compute-bound region for FP16 GEMMs at small batch/short sequences; raising SM clock improves latency until memory bandwidth becomes the limiter. Monitor DRAM bw and p99 for seq=128 to detect overclock knee.

- NVIDIA H100:
  * Baseline: h100-balanced-v1 -> utilize default SM 1500-1650 ranges depending on SKU, avoid aggressive mem overclock.
  * Latency: h100-latency-v1 -> enable higher SM clock *and* prefer the new attention kernel path (opt_kv_prefetch on) for seq<=128 requests; cap power moderately to reduce thermal-induced freq throttling.
  * Notes: H100 benefits from kernel fusion for attention; ensure the kernel selector prefers fused attention for short sequences and disables fusion fallback when under heavy memory contention. H100 thermal headroom is critical; prefer short bursts rather than long elevated clocks.

- NVIDIA L4 (inference-optimized Ampere-like):
  * Baseline: l4-balanced-v1 -> target low clocks with high efficiency; default is already power-efficient.
  * Latency: l4-latency-v1 -> raise SM clock within validated safety window; in many workloads L4 is memory-bound due to lower DRAM bandwidth, so tiling (smaller GEMM tiles, lower per-kernel working set) yields better results than brute force clock increases.
  * Notes: For L4, optimize kernel tiling ahead of clock changes. Favor int8 kernels with smaller scratch when available.

- AMD MI300:
  * Baseline: mi300-balanced-v1 -> leverage ROCm recommended clocks; avoid sustained high-power cap that causes device-level thermal governor ramp-down.
  * Latency: mi300-latency-v1 -> prioritize memory clock increases before compute clock for workloads where GEMM tiling shows memory-bound profiles.
  * Notes: MI300 has a different memory hierarchy; big MCM dies can show uneven NUMA-like behavior. Run per-socket tiling to keep KV hotsets colocated.

Tiling and KV cache interaction:
- Problem: large, dense GEMM kernels that require big scratch buffers increase device memory churn. When we evict KV pages mid-session, chat latency spikes as new context is re-paginated.
- Mitigation knobs:
  1) Conservative tiling for interactive routes: force smaller kernel tiles for interactive request lanes to keep per-call working set small. This slightly increases kernel count but reduces peak memory per-concurrent-request and KV pressure.
  2) KV affinity: attempt to colocate KV cache for long-lived sessions on GPUs that will be assigned low-power/latency profiles, and avoid colocating ephemeral batch tasks on the same GPU when possible.
  3) Eviction backpressure: add a runtime metric for 'kv-eviction-rate' and throttle batch admission when eviction > threshold.

Kernel preemption / scheduling windows:
- We propose a small preemption window for interactive kernels where long-running batch kernels can be paused (if the underlying driver supports MPS-like preemption) to guarantee interactive latency SLOs. For GPUs without reasonable preemption, prefer placement on separate cards or use kernel tiling approach to make long kernels preemptible at tile boundaries.
- Implementation TODOs:
  * Add kernel fence points in the fused attention path so an in-flight long kernel can checkpoint and yield to an interactive kernel.
  * Integrate with scheduler to mark requests as "preemptible" or "latency-sensitive" and schedule accordingly.

Calibration flow (automation):
1) Node agent pulls host SKU metadata (A100/H100/L4/MI300, PCI topology, mem size).
2) Run microbench harness with representative job mix. Sweep clocks/power caps in prioritized order (clock up/down, then power cap adjust).
3) Evaluate candidate profiles against constraints: p99 improvement, kv-eviction delta <=2%, watts/token delta.
4) Upload named profile artifact to control plane and tag with hardware fingerprint + timestamp.
5) Rollout via existing deployment orchestration with canary.

Safety, thermals, and reliability considerations:
- Never set clocks above vendor validated safe ranges; always cross-check with vendor utilities (nvidia-smi --query-supported-clocks).
- Watch for sustained Tjunction increases; include a thermal rollback rule that restores balanced profile if GPU temp > 85C for > 30s.
- In mixed rack-level power provisioning, coordinate host-level power caps so that raising clock on a host does not starve the PDU budget for neighbors.

Monitoring & observability (required metrics):
- per-host/profile: current-profile, applied-clock, applied-power-cap, house-keeping-uptime
- kernel-level: kernel-id, kernel-latency histogram, kernel-memory-bytes, kernel-sm-util
- kv-cache: resident-size, eviction-rate, miss-latency
- thermal/power: gpu-temp, package-power, fan-speed

Rollout plan (short):
- Stage 0 (this doc): internal review with serving-runtime and infra/planet teams.
- Stage 1 (lab): run calibration on 2 hosts per SKU and validate metrics with synthetic mixed load.
- Stage 2 (canary): deploy profiles to 5% of live capacity (latency-critical services only). Observe 2 weeks.
- Stage 3 (gradual): expand if p99 and watts/token targets met.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Kernel-land: can we add explicit tile-boundary preemption with vendor driver support? (action: engineering spike, owner: Lina).
- Calibration frequency: how often should we re-run (monthly vs on-hardware-firmware-change)? (action: infra + ops).
- Integration: surface profile selection in the route configuration so product teams can opt-in for interactive vs batch profiles. (action: product + api).

Appendix: quick checklist for lab calibration run
- Snapshot host firmware and driver versions.
- Lock other background jobs.
- Load model and prime KV cache with standard hotset.
- Run sequence-length sweep and capture metrics to CSV.
- Run power cap sweep in steps of 5% and capture watts/token.
- Save profile artifact and attach CSV and perf.log to PR.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on per-GPU clock ranges. We prefer incremental wins that are observable.
- We should align with platform-engineering on rack-level power headroom before fleet wide changes.

End of draft.
